## 4 Lower Bounds for Listing Cliques

In this section, we will show our conditional lower bound for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ under the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis.

#### Theorem 4.1 (Theorem 1.10).

For any $k\geq 3,1\leq\ell<k$ , and $\gamma\in[0,k/\ell]$ , $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for instances with $t=\tilde{\Theta}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma})$ requires

$$ \left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-o(1)} $$

time, where $\Delta_{\ell}$ is the number of $\ell$ -cliques and $t$ is the number of $k$ -cliques required to list, assuming Hypothesis 1.3.

#### Proof.

First, we can assume $\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}+\gamma(1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)})>1$ , as otherwise the lower bound is trivial.

Let $G=(V=V_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_{k},E,w)$ be a $k$ -partite Exact- $k$ -Clique instance on $k\cdot n$ nodes. Without loss of generality, we assume the edge weights $w$ of $G$ are from $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for some sufficiently large prime $p=n^{O(k)}=n^{O(1)}$ . Then we sample $x\sim\mathbb{F}_{p}$ uniformly at random. For every $i\in[k]$ , and every node $v\in V_{i}$ , we sample $k-1$ random variables $(y_{v,j})_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}\sim\mathbb{F}_{p}$ where $\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{v,j}=0$ uniformly at random. Note that $(y_{v,j})_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}$ are $(k-2)$ -wise independent.

For every $1\leq i<j\leq k$ , and $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ , let

$$ w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})=x\cdot w(v_{i},v_{j})+y_{v_{i},j}+y_{v_{j},i}. $$

It is not difficult to verify that, whenever $x\neq 0$ , the sets of exact- $k$ -cliques in the graph with weight $w$ and with weight $w^{\prime}$ are the same.

Then we partition $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ into $s$ contiguous intervals, each of length $O(p/s)$ , for some $s$ to be chosen later where $\Omega(1)\leq s\leq O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ . Consider all combinations of intervals $(L_{i,j})_{1\leq i<j\leq k}$ , where $0\in\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}L_{i,j}$ . If we fix an arbitrary choice of the first $\binom{k}{2}-1$ intervals, their sumset is an interval of length $O(p/s)$ . Thus, there is only $O(1)$ choices for the last interval in order for their sumset to contain $0$ . Hence, there are only $O(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1})$ such combinations. For each such combination, we construct an instance of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ as follows: create an unweighted graph $H$ such that an edge $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ for $i<j$ in $G$ is added to $H$ if and only if $w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\in L_{i,j}$ . The high level idea then is to list a certain number of $k$ -cliques in $H$ and verify whether any of them is an exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . Clearly, this algorithm never finds an exact- $k$ -clique if $G$ does not have one, so it suffices to show that when $G$ does have an exact- $k$ -clique, the algorithm finds it with decent probability.

Let $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ be an arbitrary exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . Clearly, there exists one combination of intervals such that all edges in this exact- $k$ -clique are in the corresponding subgraph $H_{0}$ . For any $i,j$ and edge $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ , the edge is in $H_{0}$ only if $w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\in[-O(p/s),O(p/s)]$ , which happens with probability $O(1/s)$ as long as $\{u_{i},u_{j}\}\neq\{v_{i},v_{j}\}$ . The following lemma shows that the random variables $w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})$ are fairly independent.

#### Lemma 4.2.

If $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ is not an exact- $k$ -clique w.r.t. $w$ , and $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ shares exactly $c$ nodes indexed by $S$ with $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ , then the random variables

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<j\leq k\\
i\not\in S\text{ or }j\not\in S\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

#### Proof.

By symmetry, we can assume $|S|=[c]$ , and we need to show that

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}=\left\{x\cdot(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j}))+y_{u_{i},j}+y_{u_{j},i}-y_{v_{i},j}-y_{v_{j},i}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

Define $\alpha_{i,j}=w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})$ . Let $\beta$ be the sum of all the $\alpha_{i,j}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\beta \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}\alpha_{i,j}=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\alpha_{i,j} \displaystyle=x\cdot\left(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{u_{i},j}-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{v_{i},j} \displaystyle=x\cdot\left(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\right). $$

Since $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ is an exact- $k$ -clique whereas $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ is not, we have $\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\neq 0$ . Therefore, $\beta$ is uniformly random.

Showing $\left\{\alpha_{i,j}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are independent is equivalent to showing that the variables are independent when one of the variables is replaced with the sums of the variables. Namely, it suffices to show $\left\{\alpha_{i,j}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\\ (i,j)\neq(k-1,k)\end{subarray}}\cup\{\beta\}$ are independent.

Consider the following ordering of the variables:

$$ \beta,\alpha_{c+1,1},\ldots,\alpha_{c+1,c},\alpha_{c+2,1},\ldots,\alpha_{c+2,c+1},\ldots,\alpha_{k-1,1},\ldots,\alpha_{k-1,k-2},\alpha_{k,1},\ldots,\alpha_{k,k-2}. $$

Conditioned on the previous variables, all $\alpha_{j,i}$ variables in this list has an additive term $y_{u_{j},i}$ that is independent of all previous variables. Thus, this list of variables is independent. ∎

#### Corollary 4.3.

For any $\ell$ -clique on nodes $(v_{i})_{i\in T}$ in $G$ that shares exactly $c$ nodes indexed by $S$ with $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ , the random variables

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in T\\
i<j\\
i\not\in S\text{ or }j\not\in S\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

#### Proof.

By symmetry, we can assume $[T]=[\ell]$ and $[S]=[c]$ . We can complete this $\ell$ -clique to a nonzero $k$ -clique $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ (we can assume any $\ell$ -clique is in some nonzero $k$ -clique by adding hypothetical nodes to the graph in this analysis).

By Lemma 4.2, $\left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are independent, so $\left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq\ell\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are also independent. ∎

Now we can compute the expected number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ . The number of $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ that share exactly $c$ nodes with $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ is $O(n^{\ell-c})$ . By Corollary 4.3, each of them is in $H_{0}$ with probability $O\left(1/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}-\binom{c}{2}}\right)$ . Therefore, the expected number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is

$$ O\left(\sum_{c=0}^{\ell}n^{\ell-c}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}-\binom{c}{2}}\right)=O\left(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}\right), $$

since by our choice of $s=O(n^{2/(k-1)})$ , we have that $s^{\binom{c}{2}}=O(n^{c})$ .

Similarly, the expected number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is $O\left(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}\right)$ .

Therefore, by Markov’s inequality and union bound, with probability at least $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , the number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is at most $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ and the number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is at most $n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}$ .

Let $s=n^{\frac{k-\gamma\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\gamma\binom{\ell}{2}}}$ , so that $\frac{n^{k}}{s^{\binom{k}{2}}}=\left(\frac{n^{\ell}}{s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}}\right)^{\gamma}$ . We can verify that indeed $\Omega(1)\leq s\leq O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ . In fact, since $\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}+\gamma(1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)})>1$ , we can obtain a stronger upper bound $s=O\left(n^{\frac{k-\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}-1}-\delta}\right)$ for $\delta>0$ .

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is a $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ for instances with specified $t=\tilde{\Theta}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma})$ with running time

$$ T(\Delta_{\ell},t)=O\left(\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-{\varepsilon}}\right) $$

for some ${\varepsilon}>0$ . Then consider the following algorithm for Exact- $k$ -Clique:

- 1. First, hash the weights of the graph and enumerate $O(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1})$ graphs $H$ as described earlier.

- 2. Enumerate all $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ , and pre-compute which graphs $H$ contain each $\ell$ -clique. Since each $\ell$ -clique exists in $s^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}$ graphs $H$ , and this list of graphs can be listed efficiently, this step costs

$$ \tilde{O}\left(n^{\ell}\cdot s^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)\leq\tilde{O}\left(n^{\ell}\cdot\left(n^{\frac{k-\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}-1}-\delta}\right)^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)\leq\tilde{O}(n^{k-\delta^{\prime}}) $$

for some $\delta^{\prime}>0$ .

- 3. From the previous step, we have a list of $\ell$ -cliques for each graph $H$ . If some $H$ contains more than $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ $\ell$ -cliques, we skip it. If it contains fewer than $0.99n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ $\ell$ -cliques, we add a complete $\ell$ -partite graphs with $n^{\prime}$ nodes on each part, for some $n^{\prime}$ , so that the total number of $\ell$ -cliques in the new graph reaches $0.99(n+n^{\prime})^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ . Clearly, $n^{\prime}=O(n)$ .

- 4. For graphs $H$ which we did not skip in the previous step, we run $\mathcal{A}$ on it with $t=n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}+1$ . For any $k$ -clique listed by $\mathcal{A}$ , we test whether it is an exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . This step takes $s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\cdot T(\tilde{O}(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}),\tilde{O}(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}))$ time.

- 5. If any exact- $k$ -clique is found in the previous step, we return YES for the Exact- $k$ -Clique instance; otherwise, we return NO.

Clearly, if $G$ contains no exact- $k$ -clique, our algorithm is always correct. If $G$ contains any exact- $k$ -clique, let $H_{0}$ be the constructed graph containing it. As discussed previously, with probability $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , the number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is at most $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ and the number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is at most $n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}$ . In this case, we will not skip $H_{0}$ in Step 3, and listing $t=n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}+1$ $k$ -cliques in Step 4 guarantees an exact- $k$ -clique. Thus, we will find an exact- $k$ -clique with probability $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , which can be boosted to $1-1/\mathop{\rm poly}(n)$ by repeating the algorithm $O(\log n)$ times.

Overall, this algorithm only needs time (besides the previous $\tilde{O}(n^{k-\delta^{\prime}})$ time)

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\cdot\left(\left(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}\left(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}\right)^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-{\varepsilon}}\right)=\tilde{O}\left(n^{k}\cdot\left(\frac{s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}}{n^{k}}\right)^{\varepsilon}\right). $$

As $s=O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ , the above running time can be further upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(n^{k}\cdot\left(\frac{(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})^{\binom{k}{2}-1}}{n^{k}}\right)^{\varepsilon}\right)=\tilde{O}\left(n^{k-\frac{2{\varepsilon}}{k-1}}\right), $$

contradicting the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis. ∎

## 5 Optimal Listing Algorithms for Graphs with Many $k$ -Cliques

In this section, we give a $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm that is optimal for graphs with many $k$ -cliques under Hypothesis 1.3. This algorithm can be seen as a generalization of the densifying and sparsifying paradigm of [bjorklund2014listing].

We then show how we can extend this algorithm to obtain the conditionally optimal algorithms for all $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for graphs with many $k$ -cliques.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Suppose $\omega=2$ . Then, given a graph $G$ with $t$ 4-cliques,

- • $(4,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}(n^{3}+n^{2/3}t^{5/6})$ if $G$ has $n$ nodes.

$$ D(n,t)\leq D(n,n^{2},t)\leq\tilde{O}(n^{3}+\lambda n^{2})+S(6t/\lambda,t). $$

assuming $\omega=2$ .

$$ \displaystyle D(n,t) \displaystyle\leq n^{3}+\lambda n^{2}+S(6t/\lambda,t) \displaystyle\leq n^{3}+\lambda n^{2}+\frac{tx}{\lambda}+\frac{tx^{2/3}}{\lambda^{1/3}}+D\left(\frac{12t}{\lambda x},t\right) $$

#### Claim 5.3.

For any $k\geq 3$ , $x_{k}=x_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k}{k-1}\cdot((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)$ and $y_{k}=(3-\omega)\cdot y_{k-1}+x_{k-1}$ .

#### Theorem 5.4.

$$ \displaystyle S(m,t) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}T_{k-1}(\deg(v),\Delta_{k}(v))+D(2m/x,t). \displaystyle\leq\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\left(\deg(v)^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)}+\deg(v)^{\alpha_{k-1}}\Delta_{k}(v)^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}\right)+D(2m/x,t). $$

One can use Hölder’s inequality as in Corollary 2.2 to bound

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\deg(v)^{\alpha_{k-1}}\Delta_{k}(v)^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} \displaystyle\leq x^{\alpha_{k-1}-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\deg(v)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}\Delta_{k}(v)^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} \displaystyle\leq x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}\left(\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\deg(v)\right)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}\left(\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\Delta_{k}(v)\right)^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} \displaystyle\leq O\left(x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}m^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}\right). $$

Thus, we have that (once again ignoring $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors)

$$ S(m,t)\leq m\cdot x^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)-1}+x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}m^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}+D(2m/x,t). $$

Unravelling the runtime of ${\tt Dense}(G,n,t)$ , we therefore have

$$ \displaystyle D(n,t)\leq \displaystyle n^{k-3+\omega}+\lambda^{3-\omega}n^{\omega(k-2)-2k+6} \displaystyle+(t/\lambda)\cdot x^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)-1}+x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}(t/\lambda)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} \displaystyle+D\left(\frac{2\cdot\binom{k}{2}t}{\lambda x},t\right). $$

If one chooses $\lambda$ and $x$ so that $\frac{2\cdot\binom{k}{2}t}{\lambda x}\leq\frac{n}{2}$ , then the runtime is dominated by the first 4 terms up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors. Therefore, we choose $\lambda=\max\{1,\frac{4\cdot\binom{k}{2}t}{nx}\}$ (note that for $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ , this value will always be equal to $\frac{4\cdot\binom{k}{2}t}{nx}$ for our setting of $x$ ). Hence, ignoring $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors, this gives us for $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle D(n,t) \displaystyle\leq n^{k-3+\omega}+\left(\frac{t}{nx}\right)^{3-\omega}n^{\omega(k-2)-2k+6} \displaystyle+(n\cdot x)\cdot x^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)-1}+x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}(n\cdot x)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} $$

First, suppose that the term $\left(\frac{t}{nx}\right)^{3-\omega}n^{\omega(k-2)-2k+6}$ dominates $n^{k-3+\omega}$ and the term $x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}(n\cdot x)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}$ dominates $(n\cdot x)\cdot x^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)-1}$ (we show that this is in fact true for our choice of $\gamma_{k}$ later) . Then,

$$ D(n,t)\leq\left(\frac{t}{nx}\right)^{3-\omega}n^{\omega(k-2)-2k+6}+x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}(n\cdot x)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}. $$

Choosing $x$ to equate the two terms, we set

$$ x=\left({t^{\alpha_{k-1}-(\omega-2)(k-1)}n^{(k-1)^{2}\omega-(\alpha_{k-1}+2k^{2}-5k+3)}}\right)^{\frac{1}{(k-1)(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}}. $$

Substituting this into (3), we have

$$ D(n,t)\leq n^{\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}}t^{\frac{(3-\omega)((k-2)\alpha_{k-1}+(k-1))}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}}. $$

Setting

$$ \alpha_{k}=\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}, $$

it is easy to verify that the above bound is in fact of the form $n^{\alpha_{k}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{k}}.$ Moreover, note that

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{k} \displaystyle=\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)} \displaystyle=\frac{k\cdot\frac{x_{k-1}}{y_{k-1}}\cdot((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3-\omega+\frac{x_{k-1}}{y_{k-1}})} \displaystyle=\frac{x_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k}{k-1}\cdot((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(3-\omega)\cdot y_{k-1}+x_{k-1}}=\frac{x_{k}}{y_{k}} $$

as desired.

#### Bound on $\gamma_{k}$ .

Now, it suffices to show that for $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ , for our choice of $x$ ,

$$ \displaystyle n^{k-3+\omega} \displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{t}{nx}\right)^{3-\omega}n^{\omega(k-2)-2k+6}=n^{\alpha_{k}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{k}} \displaystyle(n\cdot x)\cdot x^{\alpha_{k-1}+\gamma_{k-1}\left(1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}\right)-1} \displaystyle\leq x^{\alpha_{k-1}\cdot\frac{k-2}{k-1}}(n\cdot x)^{\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k-1}}{k-1}} $$

The first inequality (6) is trivially satisfied since we chose $\gamma_{k}\geq k\left(1-\frac{3-\omega}{k-\alpha_{k}}\right).$

It suffices to show that the second inequality (7) is also satisfied. Rearranging, we see that it suffices to show that $x^{\gamma_{k-1}}\leq\frac{t}{n}.$ Plugging in $x$ from (4) and $\gamma_{k-1}$ and rearranging, we obtain that this holds as long as

$$ t\geq n^{\frac{(k-1)\cdot((3-\omega)^{2}+k(\omega-2))+\alpha_{k-1}(k(2-\omega)+\omega-3)}{11-(\omega-2)\alpha_{k-1}+k(\omega-2)-7\omega+\omega^{2}}}. $$

To show that all $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ satisfies the above inequality, it suffices to check that the exponent above is at most $\gamma_{k}$ , i.e., it suffices to check that

$$ \frac{(k-1)\cdot((3-\omega)^{2}+k(\omega-2))+\alpha_{k-1}(k(2-\omega)+\omega-3)}{(k-1-\alpha_{k-1})(\omega-2)+(3-\omega)^{2}}\leq\gamma_{k}=k\left(1-\frac{3-\omega}{k-\alpha_{k}}\right). $$

If $\omega=2$ , we can rewrite (5) as $\alpha_{k}=\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}}{(k-1)(1+\alpha_{k-1})}$ to obtain the following equivalent inequality:

$$ \displaystyle k-(\alpha_{k-1}+1)\leq k-\frac{(k-1)}{(k-1)+(k-2)\alpha_{k-1}}\cdot(\alpha_{k-1}+1), $$

which clearly holds since $(k-2)\alpha_{k-1}\geq 0.$

When $\omega>2$ , we substitute our recursive formula for $\alpha_{k}$ from (5) and rearrange to obtain that the inequality is satisfied for all $k>0$ as long as

$$ \displaystyle(k-1)(\omega-2)\leq\alpha_{k-1}\leq k-1+\frac{(3-\omega)^{2}}{\omega-2}. $$

#### Claim 5.5.

For $2\leq\omega\leq 3$ and $k\geq 2$ , we have $k(\omega-2)\leq\alpha_{k}$ .

#### Proof.

We show this by induction. When $k=2$ , the equation is clearly true because $0\leq\omega-2\leq 1$ . Therefore, $2(\omega-2)\leq 2,$ and the lower bound clearly holds.

Now suppose $k\geq 3$ and that $\alpha_{k-1}\geq(k-1)(\omega-2)$ . Now, we want $\alpha_{k}\geq k(\omega-2)$ . Substituting the recursion from (5), we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}\geq k(\omega-2). $$

Rearranging the equation using the fact that $3-\omega+\alpha_{k-1}>0$ , we have that the above equation holds if and only if

$$ \displaystyle(3-\omega)(\alpha_{k-1}-(k-1)(\omega-2))\geq 0. $$

Since $\omega\leq 3$ and $\alpha_{k-1}\geq(k-1)(\omega-2)$ , we have that the equation indeed holds. ∎

#### Claim 5.6.

For $2\leq\omega\leq 3$ and $k\geq 2$ , $\alpha_{k}\leq k.$

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction. First, we note that $\alpha_{2}=2$ and $\alpha_{3}=\frac{3(\omega-1)}{5-\omega}\leq 3$ since $\omega\leq 3$ . Now, suppose $\alpha_{k-1}\leq k-1$ . Then, note that

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{k} \displaystyle\leq\frac{k\alpha_{k-1}((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{(k-1)\cdot(3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega)}\leq\frac{k((5-2k)+(k-2)\omega)}{3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega}. $$

Therefore, $\alpha_{k}\leq k$ as long as

$$ \displaystyle(5-2k)+(k-2)\omega\leq 3+\alpha_{k-1}-\omega \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle\alpha_{k-1}\geq(k-1)(\omega-2), $$

which is indeed true by Claim 5.5. ∎

Therefore, the bounds in (8) indeed hold, thereby completing the proof. ∎

Using the bound of Theorem 5.4 and note that the runtime of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ is monotone with respect to $t$ (Lemma 2.7), we immediately get the following corollaries.

#### Corollary 5.7 (Theorem 1.5).

Given a graph on $n$ nodes, one can list $t$ 4-cliques in

$$ \tilde{O}\left(n^{\omega+1}+n^{\frac{4(\omega-1)(2\omega-3)}{\omega^{2}-5\omega+12}}t^{1-\frac{(\omega-1)(2\omega-3)}{\omega^{2}-5\omega+12}}\right) $$

time. If $\omega=2$ , the runtime is $\tilde{O}(n^{3}+n^{2/3}t^{5/6}).$

#### Corollary 5.8 (Theorem 1.6).

Given a graph on $n$ nodes, one can list $t$ 5-cliques in

$$ \tilde{O}\left(n^{\omega+2}+n^{\frac{5(\omega-1)(2\omega-3)(3\omega-5)}{48-47\omega+16\omega^{2}-\omega^{3}}}t^{1-\frac{(\omega-1)(2\omega-3)(3\omega-5)}{48-47\omega+16\omega^{2}-\omega^{3}}}\right) $$

time. If $\omega=2$ , the runtime is $\tilde{O}(n^{4}+n^{1/2}t^{9/10}).$

### 5.4 Analysis for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for $\ell\geq 2$

We have shown an algorithm for $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ that is conditionally optimal when $\Delta_{k}\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ . Now, we use this to show that there exists a $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm for all $\ell$ that is conditionally optimal for $\Delta_{k}\geq n^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ , for some $0\leq\gamma_{k,\ell}<\frac{k}{\ell}.$ First, we define the following variable

$$ z_{k,\ell}=x_{k}\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}\frac{k-\ell}{k-i-1}\cdot\frac{y_{k-i}}{x_{k-i}} $$

where $x_{k}$ and $y_{k}$ are just as defined in (1) and (2). From this definition, the following identity is immediate.

#### Claim 5.9.

For $\ell\geq 2$ and $k>\ell$ , $z_{k,\ell}=\frac{x_{k}}{x_{k-1}}z_{k-1,\ell-1}+\frac{k-\ell}{k-1}y_{k}$ .

#### Theorem 5.10.

Fix any constant integers $k-1\geq\ell\geq 1$ . Let $\alpha_{k,\ell}=x_{k}/z_{k,\ell}$ . Then, there exists some $\gamma_{k,\ell}=(1-\varepsilon_{k,\ell})k/\ell$ for $\varepsilon_{k,\ell}>0$ such that for large $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ there exists an algorithm that lists all $t$ $k$ -cliques given the $\ell$ -cliques in time $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\alpha_{k,\ell}}t^{1-\frac{\ell\alpha_{k,\ell}}{k}})$ .

If $\omega=2$ , we have $x_{k}=k$ and $z_{k,\ell}=\frac{k\ell(k-\ell)}{2}$ , giving a runtime of $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}})$ for all $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ , where

$$ \gamma_{k,\ell}=\frac{k(k^{2}-2k-1)}{\ell(k^{2}-k-\ell-1)}. $$

#### Proof.

We show this inductively on $\ell$ . For $\ell=1$ , we have $z_{k,1}=y_{k}$ , and this simply reduces to Theorem 5.4.

For some $\ell>1$ , suppose that the theorem statement is true for all $\ell^{\prime}<\ell$ and $k^{\prime}>\ell^{\prime}$ . In particular, we assume that $(k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ takes time

$$ \tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}\Delta_{k^{\prime}}^{1-\frac{\ell^{\prime}\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}{k^{\prime}}}) $$

for $\Delta_{k^{\prime}}\geq\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\gamma_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}},$ and that the runtime is

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}+\gamma_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}\left(1-\frac{\ell^{\prime}\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}{k^{\prime}}\right)}\right) $$

for $\Delta_{k^{\prime}}\leq\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\gamma_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}.$ We may assume this because the runtime is non-decreasing in $\Delta_{k^{\prime}}$ by Lemma 2.7.

Recall that, at a high level, Algorithm 5.1 first lists all $k$ -cliques containing nodes that are contained in at most $x$ $\ell$ -cliques, and deletes all such nodes. Now, there are at most $k\Delta_{\ell}/x$ nodes left in the graph, and we call the ${\tt Dense}$ algorithm from Algorithm 5.1.

#### Runtime analysis.

Fix any $k>\ell$ . In Step 2 of the algorithm, the runtime is given by (omitting $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors):

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{v:\Delta_{\ell}(v)\leq x}\left(\Delta_{\ell}(v)^{\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}+\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}\left(1-\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}\right)}+\Delta_{\ell}(v)^{\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}\Delta_{k}(v)^{1-\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}\right) \displaystyle\leq\Delta_{\ell}x^{\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}+\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}\left(1-\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}\right)-1}+\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}x^{\frac{(k-\ell)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}, $$

where we use Hölder’s inequality to bound the second term. Suppose for now that $t$ is large enough so that the second term dominates.

In Step 4, by Theorem 5.4, the runtime can be bounded by $(k\Delta_{\ell}/x)^{\alpha_{k}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{k}}$ up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors, if we have

$$ t\geq(\Delta_{\ell}/x)^{\gamma_{k}}. $$

Suppose that $t$ is large enough so that this inequality holds. Then, the runtime of the algorithm is

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}t^{1-\frac{(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}x^{\frac{(k-\ell)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{k-1}}+\left(\frac{\Delta_{\ell}}{x}\right)^{\alpha_{k}}t^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k}}{k}}. $$

Choosing

$$ x=\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{(k-1)\alpha_{k}-(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}{(k-1)\alpha_{k}+(k-\ell)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}}}t^{\frac{k(\ell-1)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}-(k-1)\alpha_{k}}{k((k-1)\alpha_{k}+(k-\ell)\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1})}}, $$

we get a runtime of (omitting $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors)

$$ \Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{\alpha_{k}\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-1)}{\alpha_{k}(k-1)+\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-\ell))}}t^{1-\frac{\ell}{k}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{k}\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-1)}{\alpha_{k}(k-1)+\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-\ell))}}, $$

therefore giving

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{k,\ell} \displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{k}\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-1)}{\alpha_{k}(k-1)+\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}(k-\ell)} \displaystyle=\frac{\frac{x_{k}}{y_{k}}\cdot\frac{x_{k-1}}{z_{k-1,\ell-1}}}{\frac{x_{k}}{y_{k}}+\frac{k-\ell}{k-1}\cdot\frac{x_{k-1}}{z_{k-1,\ell-1}}} \displaystyle=\frac{x_{k}}{\frac{x_{k}}{x_{k-1}}z_{k-1,\ell-1}+\frac{k-\ell}{k-1}\cdot y_{k}}=\frac{x_{k}}{z_{k,\ell}} $$

by Claim 5.9.

#### Bound on $\gamma_{k,\ell}$ if $\omega=2$ .

If $\ell=1$ , then $\gamma_{k,1}$ matches the value of $\gamma_{k}$ we obtained from Theorem 5.4. Thus, we assume $\ell>1$ and the bound for all $\ell^{\prime}<\ell$ holds. Recall that when $\omega=2$ , $\alpha_{k}=\frac{2}{k-1}$ and $\alpha_{k-1,\ell-1}=\frac{2}{(\ell-1)(k-\ell)}$ . Therefore, substituting this into (11), we obtain

$$ x=\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{(k-\ell-1)(\ell-1)}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{\frac{\ell-1}{k(k-\ell)}}. $$

First, we check that (10) holds. In fact,

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\left(\frac{\Delta_{\ell}}{x}\right)^{\gamma_{k}}=\left(\Delta_{\ell}\cdot\Delta_{\ell}^{-\frac{(k-\ell-1)(\ell-1)}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{-\frac{\ell-1}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}} \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle t^{1+\frac{\gamma_{k}(\ell-1)}{k(k-\ell)}}\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{(k-1)\gamma_{k}}{\ell(k-\ell)}} \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k(k-1)\gamma_{k}}{k\ell(k-\ell)+\ell(\ell-1)\gamma_{k}}}. $$

Substituting $\gamma_{k}=k-1-\frac{2}{k^{2}-k-2}$ from Theorem 5.4, we get the inequality $t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k(k^{2}-2k-1)}{\ell(k^{2}-k-\ell-1)}}=\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ , which is indeed true by our choice of $\gamma_{k,\ell}$ .

Now, it suffices to show that if $t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ , then the second term dominates in (9). In fact, the second term dominates as long as

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}x^{\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1} \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{1+\frac{(k-\ell-1)(\ell-1)}{\ell(k-\ell)}(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)}{1-\frac{\ell-1}{k(k-\ell)}(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)}}=\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k(k-1)(k-3)}{\ell(k^{2}-3k+3-\ell)}}, $$

where the last equality holds because $\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}=\frac{(k-1)((k-1)^{2}-2(k-1)-1)}{(\ell-1)((k-1)^{2}-k-\ell+1)}$ by induction. Hence, it suffices to show that $\gamma_{k,\ell}$ is at least the exponent on the right-hand side.

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{k,\ell}=\frac{k(k^{2}-2k-1)}{\ell(k^{2}-k-\ell-1)}\geq\frac{k(k-1)(k-3)}{\ell(k^{2}-3k+3-\ell)} \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle 1-\frac{k-\ell}{k^{2}-k-1-\ell}\geq 1-\frac{k-\ell}{k^{2}-3k-\ell+3} \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle k^{2}-k-1-\ell\geq k^{2}-3k-\ell+3 \displaystyle\iff \displaystyle k\geq 2, $$

which is true since $k\geq 3.$

#### Bound on $\gamma_{k,\ell}$ if $\omega>2$ .

In this case, we show that there exists some $\varepsilon_{k,\ell}>0$ such that $\gamma_{k,\ell}\leq\frac{k}{\ell}(1-\varepsilon_{k,\ell})$ .

First, consider (10). Note that one can rewrite

$$ \displaystyle x=\Delta_{\ell}^{1-\frac{\alpha_{k,\ell}}{\alpha_{k}}}t^{\frac{\ell\alpha_{k,\ell}}{k\alpha_{k}}-\frac{1}{k}}. $$

Rewriting $q=\frac{\alpha_{k,\ell}}{\alpha_{k}}$ , and substituting this into (10), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\left(\frac{\Delta_{\ell}}{x}\right)^{\gamma_{k}}=\left(\frac{\Delta_{\ell}^{q}}{t^{\frac{\ell q}{k}-\frac{1}{k}}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}}\iff t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{kq\gamma_{k}}{\ell q\gamma_{k}+k-\gamma_{k}}}. $$

By choosing $\varepsilon_{1}=\frac{k-\gamma_{k}}{\ell q\gamma_{k}+k-\gamma_{k}}$ (which is positive since $k>\gamma_{k}$ by Theorem 5.10, it is easy to check that the right-hand side is equal to $\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k}{\ell}(1-\varepsilon_{1})}$ .

Now, consider (9). For the second term to dominate, we can rewrite the inequality as

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}\cdot x^{\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1}=\Delta_{\ell}^{1+(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)(1-q)}t^{\frac{1}{k}\cdot(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)(\ell q-1)}. $$

Rearranging this, we see that we require

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{1+(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)(1-q)}{1-\frac{1}{k}(\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}-1)(\ell q-1)}}. $$

By the induction hypothesis, we know there exists some $0<\varepsilon^{\prime}<1$ such that $\gamma_{k-1,\ell-1}=\frac{k-1}{\ell-1}(1-\varepsilon^{\prime}).$ Therefore, substituting this into the above equation and rearranging, we require

$$ \displaystyle t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k}{\ell}\left(1-\frac{(k-1)(\ell-1)\varepsilon^{\prime}}{(q\ell-1)(k-1)\varepsilon^{\prime}+\ell((k-1)-q(k-\ell))}\right)}. $$

Let $\varepsilon_{num}=(k-1)(\ell-1)\varepsilon^{\prime}$ and and $\varepsilon_{den}=(q\ell-1)(k-1)\varepsilon^{\prime}+\ell((k-1)-q(k-\ell))$ . Clearly, since $k\geq 3$ and $\ell\geq 2$ , $\varepsilon_{num}>0$ . Now, consider two cases.

- • $q\ell-1\geq 0$ . Then, since $\varepsilon^{\prime}>0$ , we have $\varepsilon_{den}\geq\ell((k-1)-q(k-\ell))>0$ since $q=\frac{\alpha_{k,\ell}}{\alpha_{k}}=\frac{y_{k}}{z_{k,\ell}}<\frac{k-1}{k-\ell}$ by Claim 5.9.

- • $q\ell-1<0$ . Then, since $\varepsilon^{\prime}<1,$ $\ell\geq 2,$ $q>0$ and $k\geq 3$ $\displaystyle\varepsilon_{den}$ $\displaystyle>(q\ell-1)(k-1)+\ell((k-1)-q(k-\ell))$ $\displaystyle=q\ell(\ell-1)+(\ell-1)(k-1)>0.$

Therefore, let $\varepsilon_{2}=\frac{\varepsilon_{num}}{\varepsilon_{den}}$ . Clearly, $\varepsilon_{2}>0$ . Then, if $t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{k}{\ell}(1-\varepsilon_{2})}$ , then (12) holds. Hence, we can pick $\varepsilon_{k,\ell}=\min\{\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}\}>0$ to ensure both conditions (9) and (10) hold. ∎

## 6 Extending the Algorithm to Graphs with Fewer $k$ -Cliques

In this section, we show how to apply our algorithm in Section 5 which only works for very large $t$ (or rather, does not have improved runtime for smaller $t$ ) to other ranges of $t$ as well, via black-box reductions.

#### Theorem 6.1.

Suppose for every $1\leq\ell<k$ , $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\alpha_{k,\ell}}t^{1-\frac{\ell\alpha_{k,\ell}}{k}})$ time when $t\geq\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ . Then for every $1\leq\ell\leq k$ and $1\leq s<k$ where $\lceil\frac{k}{s}\rceil\neq\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil$ , $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{s}{\ell}\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil}\right)^{\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}t^{1-\frac{\ell^{\prime}\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}{k^{\prime}}}\right) $$

time for $t\geq\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{s}{\ell}\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil}\right)^{\gamma_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}}$ , where $k^{\prime}=\lceil\frac{k}{s}\rceil$ and $\ell^{\prime}=\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil$ .

#### Proof.

Let $G$ be the input of a $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ instance. Without loss of generality, assume $G$ is $k$ -partite with parts $V_{1},\ldots,V_{k}$ . Create a new $k^{\prime}$ -partite graph $G^{\prime}$ on node parts $U_{1}=V_{1}\times\cdots\times V_{s},U_{2}=V_{s+1}\times\cdots\times V_{2s},\ldots,U_{k^{\prime}}=V_{s(k^{\prime}-1)+1}\times\cdots\times V_{k}$ (each node corresponds to a set of at most $s$ nodes). Keep a node $(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i})$ if and only if $(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i})$ forms a clique in $G$ . Add an edge between two nodes $(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i})$ and $(v_{1}^{\prime},v_{2}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})$ belonging to two different parts if and only if the nodes $(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i},v_{1}^{\prime},v_{2}^{\prime},\ldots,v_{i^{\prime}}^{\prime})$ form a clique in $G$ .

Clearly, $k^{\prime}$ -cliques in $G^{\prime}$ have one-to-one correspondence with $k$ -cliques in $G$ , so it suffices to list $t$ $k^{\prime}$ -cliques in $G^{\prime}$ in order to list $t$ $k$ -cliques in $G$ . Furthermore, distinct $\ell^{\prime}$ -clique in $G^{\prime}$ corresponds to distinct clique in $G$ . Depending on whether an $\ell^{\prime}$ -clique uses a node in $U_{k^{\prime}}$ , it corresponds to either an $(s\ell^{\prime})$ -clique in $G$ or an $(s\ell^{\prime}+k-sk^{\prime})$ -clique in $G$ . Either way, it is a clique of size at most $s\ell^{\prime}$ . Thus, by Lemma 2.6, there are $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{s\ell^{\prime}}{\ell}})=\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{s}{\ell}\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil})$ such cliques in $G$ and we can list them in $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{s}{\ell}\lceil\frac{\ell}{s}\rceil})$ time as well.

Thus, to solve $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ on $G$ with $t$ $k$ -cliques, it suffices to solve $(k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ on $G^{\prime}$ with $t$ $k^{\prime}$ -cliques. The theorem thus easily follows. ∎

Let us give some examples to show how to use Theorem 6.1.

First, for any $1\leq\ell\leq k$ , let us take the extreme example $s=1$ . In this case, the running time is exactly the running time given in Theorem 5.10. On the other extreme end, $s=k-1$ . Then $k^{\prime}=2$ and $\ell^{\prime}=1$ . In this extreme case, we have $\alpha_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}=2$ and $\gamma_{k^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}=0$ . Thus, we get an algorithm that works for any $t\geq 1$ , although its running time $\tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2(k-1)}{\ell}}\right)$ is not great. One can imagine when increasing $s$ from $1$ to $k-1$ , we achieve a trade-off between the bound for $t$ and running time of the algorithm.

Assume $\omega=2$ . Fix any integer $k\geq 2$ , and any integer $1\leq s<\frac{k}{2}$ . $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}\left(n^{\frac{2s}{k^{\prime}-1}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k^{\prime}(k^{\prime}-1)}}\right)$ time when $t\geq n^{s(k^{\prime}-1-\frac{2}{k^{\prime 2}-k^{\prime}-2})}$ , where $k^{\prime}=\lceil\frac{k}{s}\rceil$ .
